mcqs.question: A 1TB disk with 4KB blocks needs a bitmap of about 32MB to track free space. Why is this size acceptable?
options: It's small enough to keep resident in RAM, so scans and updates avoid disk I/O entirely
32MB is the maximum bitmap size any file system allows
The bitmap only needs to track the first 32MB of the disk
Bitmaps are always exactly 1% of disk size by design
mcqs.explanation: One bit per 4KB block scales to a small, fixed fraction of disk size — 32MB for 1TB is trivial to keep entirely in memory, making scans and updates fast. It's not a hard cap, doesn't only cover part of the disk, and the ratio follows directly from block size, not an arbitrary 1% rule.

mcqs.question: Why is finding N contiguous free blocks inherently harder with a plain linked free list than with a bitmap?
options: Linked lists cannot represent contiguous blocks at all
Linked lists only work for single-block files
Bitmaps store block addresses directly, while free lists don't store addresses
The free list must be walked node by node checking adjacency, with no shortcut to jump ahead — unlike a bitmap's direct bit scan
mcqs.explanation: A plain free list has no way to know if the next few entries are physically adjacent without walking and checking each one — an O(n) operation. A bitmap can scan for a run of zero bits directly, which is much cheaper, especially with cache-friendly bit instructions.

mcqs.question: The "counting" optimization stores `(start block, count)` pairs instead of one free-list entry per block. What real-world pattern does this exploit?
options: Free blocks are almost always scattered randomly across the disk
Free space tends to occur in contiguous runs, since files are usually allocated and freed as adjacent block ranges
Disk controllers require free blocks to be counted in groups of ten
It eliminates the need for any free space tracking structure at all
mcqs.explanation: Because files are typically allocated in adjacent runs and freed the same way, free space clusters spatially rather than scattering uniformly. Representing runs as (start, count) pairs shrinks both the metadata and the number of list entries dramatically versus one entry per block.

mcqs.question: Why do most modern general-purpose file systems (ext4, NTFS) use bitmaps rather than linked free lists for tracking free space?
options: Linked lists are illegal under the POSIX standard
Bitmaps require no memory at all, unlike free lists
Free lists cannot be used with journaling file systems
Bitmaps give fast contiguous-run lookups, O(1) free-space counting, and bounded space overhead regardless of fragmentation
mcqs.explanation: Bitmaps win on nearly every practical axis: fixed, small overhead, fast contiguous scans, and trivial total-free-space tracking. Free lists degrade under fragmentation and need extra structure (grouping/counting) just to compete. Neither claim about POSIX legality or journaling compatibility is accurate.

mcqs.question: Why must a bitmap update and the block allocation it represents be treated as one atomic operation rather than two independent writes?
options: Atomic writes are always faster than non-atomic ones
If a crash separates them, the bitmap could still show a block as free after it was already given to a file, letting a second file claim the same block and corrupt it
The bitmap format legally requires atomicity per the file system specification
Non-atomic writes are only a problem on SSDs, not HDDs
mcqs.explanation: If the block allocation reaches disk but the bitmap update doesn't (or vice versa) before a crash, the file system's view of what's free becomes wrong — potentially handing an already-used block to a second file. This is a genuine crash-consistency hazard, unrelated to write speed or a specific hardware type, which is why it's covered by journaling.
